cur:manuscripts-sinope-cursing-fig-tree.summary: Leaving the walled city on the left, Christ in a gold mantle, accompanied by a disciple in white, stretches out his hand toward a small fig tree, pronouncing that it will bear no more fruit. Two prophets stand above their inscribed panels at either side. The miniature illustrates one of the rarest Gospel subjects in early Christian art.
facts: The manuscript's five miniatures are the Feast of Herod, the Feeding of the Five Thousand, the Feeding of the Four Thousand, the Healing of the Blind of Jericho and the Cursing of the Fig Tree.
The text is written in very large uncials in gold and silver, 15 lines to a page.

Q116411166.summary: Christ, robed and haloed, seems to float upward, reaching toward the hand of God, which emerges from the clouds holding a wreath of victory, while two angels lean in from either side. Two astonished apostles flank him, and below recline lively personifications of the Earth and the Ocean. The small plaque presents the Ascension as Christ's triumphant return to the Father, leaving the created world beneath him.
facts: The Met notes that the hand of God offering a wreath of victory is an unusual feature of this Ascension.
The figures of Earth and Ocean below allude to the physical world Christ leaves behind.
The plaque was carved in the Rhineland around 1050 and is only about 10.3 cm high.

walters:W.42.1R.summary: Inside a blue initial D on a burnished gold ground, two haloed, long-haired figures sit side by side, the Father and the Son, together holding up a disc in which the white dove of the Holy Spirit spreads its wings. The image opens Psalm 109 (110), 'Dixit Dominus Domino meo: sede a dextris meis' ('The Lord said to my Lord: sit at my right hand'), which Christian readers took as the Father speaking to the Son. It is a small, lively example of how a 13th-century Flemish illuminator made the doctrine of the Trinity visible at the head of a psalm.
facts: The Psalter was made for Jernoul de Camphaing, whose name appears in a red inscription on fol. 226r; the Walters dates it to c. 1250–1275 and places it in northeastern France, then part of Flanders.
The manuscript is now misbound and incomplete: this Psalm 109 initial appears on fol. 1r, and two of the original historiated initials (for Psalms 1 and 38) are missing.
Verse 1 of Psalm 109 (110) is quoted in the New Testament and applied to Christ (Matthew 22:44; Hebrews 1:13), which underlies its Trinitarian illustration.

walters:W.42.1R.notes: Worklist year 750 was a parsing error for '3rd quarter 13th century'. The Walters TEI places the Psalm 109 text on fols. 1r–12v of the misbound volume.

walters:71.468.summary: Mary stands in ample drapery, holding the Christ Child, who reaches up to embrace her, while her left foot rests on the head of a serpent coiled before her. The ivory group stands on a plinth veneered in ivory and marked with the monogram MA beneath a sphere and cross. The image presents Mary as the new Eve, who with her Son overcomes the ancient enemy.
facts: The Walters notes that the motif of the Madonna treading on a serpent was frequent in the 17th century, when the serpent represented heresy.
The Virgin's neck and right foot have been restored, and the Child's left forearm and hand are separate pieces.
walters:71.468.notes: The worklist year (900) was wrong; the museum dates the group to the 1st quarter of the 19th century (French). Image viewed on the Walters image server.
